title: Kestrel Systems - granular KV shuffle & stream fallthrough deep dive

Agreed to run a targeted lab with KV shard tracing, longer prefix caching and repeatable load patterns; Redwood SE to provide harness and preconfigured test plan.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-22 15:00 UTC | Duration: 63 min | Attendees: Ava (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood SE), Maya (Kestrel CTO), Luca (Infra), Priya (ML Platform), Tomas (SRE)

Summary (auto): Medium-quality transcript. Technical deep dive into tail latency; multiple suggestions on KV shard routing, streaming fallthrough, and quantization collisions. Action items captured.

[00:00] Ava: OK hey everyone thanks for joining, can folks hear me?
[00:05] Maya: Yep, loud and clear, thanks.
[00:08] Diego: Hi team, I'm Diego from Redwood infra, I'll drive the deep dive, Sofia will help with repro and benchmarks.
[00:15] Priya: Quick context: our prod p95 looks fine but p99 is spiking to 600-900ms during bursts when streaming is enabled. Non-streaming calls stay under 220ms.
[00:29] Diego: Got it. First pass question — when you say streaming enabled, do you mean server-sent-chunk streaming from Redwood runtime or client-side long-polling?
[00:38] Luca: It's SSE style from your endpoint, we stream intermediate tokens. We noticed spikes align with certain prefixes — user queries that hit our personalization KV.
[00:46] Sofia: That already hints at KV hot-shard amplification. If a single prefix maps to the same KV shard and you enable streaming, you get more interleaved small requests and you can lose batching efficiency.
[00:58] Tomas: Also our VPC topology has a proxy in front, multiple NAT hops to the Redwood private endpoint; wonder if hop variance is amplifying tail.
[01:10] Diego: Right. Two axes then: application-level (KV cache sharding/hotkeys + streaming request shape) and network-level (VPC hops, cross-AZ routing). We'll step through both.

[01:35] Maya: Can we start with what the runtime does differently when streaming is on vs off? We think streaming bypasses some batching windows.
[01:44] Diego: Short answer: In our runtime streaming mode, we flush partial token buffers sooner to keep latency per token low. That reduces the available continuous-batch window which hurts throughput and increases variability for bursts. For long prefixes, the KV cache path is invoked repeatedly with smaller delta and that can expose hot-shard contention.
[02:05] Priya: Is the KV lookup synchronous on the critical path for every token? We thought it was prefetched into the KV cache.
[02:12] Sofia: By default we have prefix/KV prefetching; but there are two levels — local in-memory shard and remote shard fetch. If your affinity isn't pinned, prefetch sometimes goes to remote and you pay network hop. Also cache entries can be evicted if token sequences vary a lot, causing re-fetch.
[02:33] Luca: Our svc uses dynamic prefixes per user, so eviction is probably happening, yes.
[02:36] Diego: Exactly. We suspect a hot-shard pattern: many users hitting similar personalization keys, leads to serialization on one shard.

[03:00] [diego]: One mitigation is shard-affinity: route certain prefixes to the same GPU node persistently so that local cache hits are much higher. That requires a sticky routing layer and some overhead to rebalance.
[03:15] Maya: Rebalancing is scary for us, we can't have big reshard windows during business hours. Any non-invasive approaches?
[03:22] Sofia: You can also do prefix hashing to spread hotkeys and then locally aggregate related shards into a small LRU window. Another is to raise local LRU capacity for those prefixes — at cost of memory.
[03:34] Priya: What's the cost tradeoff? Memory vs p99?
[03:36] Diego: Ballpark: increasing per-shard LRU from 128k entries to 512k might double memory for that process but can cut remote fetch rate e.g., 10-40% depending on workload shape, which directly reduces p99. 
[03:52] Tomas: Can quantization make tail spikes worse? We run 4-bit quant on some models.
[03:59] Diego: Good question. Quantization affects kernel performance and sometimes causes extra micro-batching inside the runtime for dequant/quant folds. For 4-bit, worst-case you get slower single-token latency when the engine switches execution path, which can add tens of ms — that compounds at tail.
[04:16] Sofia: Also mixing quantized and non-quantized variants can trigger model fallback, causing longer cold-path latencies.

[04:40] [00:04:40] Maya: So if we beef up cache and avoid mixing quant modes might solve a chunk of it?
[04:46] Diego: Yes but streaming still reduces batch-ability. There's also an optimization we call stream-batching: we try to accumulate short-window token generation into micro-batches for a few ms to trade a tiny per-token latency (5-15ms) for much better p99 under load.
[04:59] Luca: Is that something we can tune on/off per-route?
[05:03] Sofia: Yes, per-route policy in Redwood console. You can pin route A as strict streaming (low latency per token, higher tail) and route B as stream-batched (slightly higher per-token but better p99).

[05:20] Tomas: On the network side, our traces show occasional 120ms spikes in NAT traversal between AZs when we run bigger bursts. Could that be dominating p99?
[05:29] Diego: Absolutely — network variance can be the dominant cost. We're seeing two patterns: 1) inter-AZ spike where one hop transiently queues, 2) packet reorder causing retries in some internal layers.
[05:41] Priya: How do we tell which one it is for our traces?
[05:44] Diego: You need hop-level timing: capture syn/ack and application-level timestamps. Our kv_shard_tracer will annotate KV fetch origin, local vs remote, and include per-hop RTTs. That helps isolate network vs runtime.

[06:10] Maya: Great. Walk us through the lab you propose.
[06:13] Diego: Plan: 1) Replay your representative prefix set (you'll send a 2k prefix sample), 2) run three modes — strict streaming, stream-batched, and non-streaming; 3) toggle KV shard affinity on/off; 4) run with quantized and non-quantized model variants. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, CPU/GPU util, and per-hop latencies.
[06:34] Sofia: We'll provide the harness (kv_shard_tracer) and a CloudFormation style template for the benchmark cluster. We recommend starting with 2 nodes (A100 equiv) and a synthetic load that mirrors your peak QPS.

[06:50] Luca: A note: our production is on-prem in a VPC-like fabric with a reverse proxy that uses pod-to-pod NAT. Is the lab able to replicate NAT variance?
[06:59] Diego: We can emulate NAT hop latency by introducing a synthetic network device in the path. Also Redwood private deployments can run the same runtime in your VPC — the behavior should match closely.
[07:10] Maya: Any quick wins we can do without the lab?
[07:14] Diego: Yes: 1) increase per-shard in-memory LRU for hot prefixes, 2) enable stream-batching for user-facing routes where one token extra latency is tolerable, 3) avoid mixing quantized variants mid-rollout, 4) pin model shard affinity for peak windows.
[07:30] Priya: For #1 is there a config flag we can flip?
[07:33] Sofia: We'll send the exact flag and default values — it's a runtime config. Diego will attach the recommended values.

[07:50] [07:50] Maya: Are there instrumentation hooks we need to add to our client to capture helpful traces?
[07:55] Diego: Prefer adding a small X-Req-Span header so the runtime echoes token-level timestamps. We'll parse that in postprocessing. Also propagate a prefix-id header so shard mapping is consistent.
[08:07] Tomas: How invasive is shard-affinity in a live environment?
[08:11] Diego: It's a routing change; low risk but you must plan rebalances. We recommend applying affinity to a subset of heavy prefixes first, monitor for heat migration, then roll out more broadly.

[08:28] Maya: Anything about batching window size? We saw docs saying 2-10ms windows.
[08:32] Sofia: Yes typical window is 4-8ms for high-throughput configs. Streaming mode reduces that to 0-2ms unless you enable stream-batching. Increasing to 6ms can reduce p99 substantially for throughput-heavy routes.
[08:45] Luca: But increasing window increases average latency, right? Our UX team will balk if token latency jumps.
[08:51] Diego: It's a tradeoff. Stream-batching tries to hit a sweet spot: add 5-10ms tail latency but reduce p99 spikes by 40-70% in some workloads. You can A/B test per route.

[09:12] [09:12] Priya: Could we combine client-side pacing to shape requests? e.g., small jittered delay so hotkeys don't align.
[09:18] Sofia: That's effective. A few ms of randomized jitter at clients can smooth hot-shard alignment. It's low-effort and often yields measurable tail improvement.

[09:30] Diego: We also ran into cases where a misconfigured proxy caused huge rebuffering on the stream path — the proxy would buffer until content-length seen and then flush. Check that your reverse proxy is stream-friendly.
[09:43] Tomas: Ours is configured for streaming but we'll re-validate.

[10:00] Maya: On the quantization front, is your recommendation to keep 4-bit on the heavy tail nodes or move to 8-bit?
[10:06] Diego: For tail-sensitive routes, 8-bit tends to be safer — less micro-path switching and more predictable single-token latency. If cost is the driver, use 4-bit for background or bulk generation routes.
[10:18] Sofia: And avoid heterogenous deployment across immediate rollouts. If a route points to both 4-bit and 8-bit variants, you can see p99 variance depending on which backend picks up the request.

[10:36] [10:36] Ava: Quick recap then?
[10:38] Diego: Root causes to investigate: 1) KV hot-shard causing remote fetches, 2) streaming reducing batching windows, 3) network/VPC hop variance, 4) quantization path switching. Proposed fixes: increase local LRU for hot prefixes, enable stream-batching where acceptable, run shard-affinity for high-volume prefixes, tune quantization per-route, add instrumentation and run lab.
[10:58] Maya: Sounds good. We'll gather the prefix sample and internal traces and upload them.

[11:05] Sofia: We'll upload the tracer and a runbook. Expect the first lab report within 6 business days after receiving traces.
[11:13] Luca: On the instrumentation, we'll add the X-Req-Span header this week.
[11:17] Tomas: I'll send a ticket linking to our VPC NAT logs.

[11:25] [11:25] Maya: Any other blockers or things we should know about secure data handling?
[11:29] Ava: For uploads use the Redwood secure link — we'll provide instructions. For Private deployment customers we can also run the lab inside your VPC so traces never leave your network.
[11:39] Priya: Excellent. When's the follow-up?
[11:42] Ava: We'll target week of Feb 2nd, 60 minute. Diego will propose slots after we get the artifacts.

[11:50] Diego: OK I'll drop the kv_shard_tracer repo link and the test template, and include recommended config booleans for stream-batching and LRU sizes.
[11:59] Maya: Thanks all, that's super helpful.
[12:02] Ava: Thanks team, we'll follow up in email with artifacts and next steps.

End of transcript.
